Ostentatious means doing something in an excessively showy way, specifically to impress other people or to draw attention to yourself. It describes a kind of display that screams "Look at me! Look at what I have! Look at how great I am!"

The key thing to understand is that ostentatious behavior is never accidental. It is always deliberate. A person who is ostentatious does not just have wealth, talent, or success — they make absolutely sure everyone around them notices it. The whole point is the audience.

Every use of this word contains two essential ingredients:

1. Excess — the display goes far beyond what is necessary or appropriate for the situation.

2. Intent to impress — the excess is not accidental; it is performed for other people's attention, admiration, or envy.

Remove either ingredient, and the word no longer fits. A genuinely wealthy person living in a large home is not necessarily ostentatious. But a person who builds a 40-room mansion with a golden gate and three fountains in a middle-class neighborhood, purely so neighbors gasp when they drive past — that is ostentatious.

Ostentatious is not a neutral word. It carries a negative, slightly mocking tone. When you call someone ostentatious, you are suggesting:

  • Their display is excessive and tasteless.
  • They are trying too hard to be admired.
  • There is something a little embarrassing or hollow about it.

It implies a lack of elegance. True class, the word suggests, does not need to shout. Ostentatious things shout constantly.

This word is flexible. It can be used to describe people, objects, behavior, and gestures.

People:
A person can be ostentatious in the way they dress, speak, or carry themselves. Someone who walks into a casual dinner party dripping in designer clothing, loudly mentioning the price of everything they are wearing, is being ostentatious.

Objects:
A car, a house, a watch, or a piece of jewelry can be described as ostentatious if it is designed or displayed primarily to signal status rather than serve a practical purpose. A watch that keeps perfect time is just a watch. A watch encrusted with diamonds worn to a job interview is ostentatious.

Behavior and gestures:
Even an act of kindness can be ostentatious. If someone donates money to a charity and then immediately issues a press release, names the building after themselves, and brings it up in every conversation, the generosity has become ostentatious. The good deed is real, but it has been weaponized for personal image.

Speech and knowledge:
A person who constantly drops difficult vocabulary words, name-drops famous people they know, or steers every conversation toward their own achievements is being ostentatious with their intellect or connections.
Vivid Examples to Lock It In

• A businessman arrives at a simple birthday lunch in a rented helicopter, wearing a fur coat, and insists the waiter announce his arrival. → Ostentatious.
  • A student answers a simple classroom question by quoting three philosophers and using ten words where two would do, purely to sound impressive. → Ostentatious.
  • A family decorates their entire house — roof, garden, fence, trees — with so many lights during the holidays that news channels come to film it. → Ostentatious.
  • A new employee at a company mentions within the first five minutes that they previously worked at three Fortune 500 companies, dropped out of Harvard voluntarily, and turned down a higher salary elsewhere. → Ostentatious.

Ostentatious ≠ simply expensive or beautiful.
A stunning painting on a wall is not ostentatious. A person who pauses every guest at the door to explain the painting's price and which famous collector they outbid to get it — that is ostentatious.

Ostentatious ≠ simply confident or proud.
Being proud of your work is natural. Ostentatious is when pride tips over into performance — when you are no longer simply confident, but are actively staging yourself for applause.

These words overlap with ostentatious and help sharpen your understanding:

  • Showy — the most casual, everyday synonym. Less sharp than ostentatious.
  • Flashy — similar, often used for clothing or style.
  • Flamboyant — can sometimes be neutral or even positive (creative, bold), unlike ostentatious.
  • Gaudy — focuses more on ugly excess of color or decoration.
  • Pretentious — about claiming importance or sophistication you do not really have.

Of all of these, ostentatious is the most precise word when you want to say: this person is deliberately putting their wealth, status, or achievements on display to impress others, and it is a bit too much.

The opposite of ostentatious is understated or modest — someone who has a great deal but does not feel the need to show it off. Old money families in many cultures are famous for being the opposite of ostentatious: they may be extraordinarily wealthy but dress plainly, drive ordinary cars, and never discuss money. That restraint is the antonym of everything ostentatious stands for.
One Sentence to Remember It Forever

Ostentatious describes any display of wealth, talent, or achievement that goes beyond what is needed — done deliberately so that other people will notice and be impressed.

If something is subtle, it is not ostentatious. If something is shown off purely for its own beauty, it is not ostentatious. But if it is excessive and performed for an audience? That is exactly what this word was made for.
